args.text: --- title: 'Hello World' description: 'Change the FHE computation in the default template so that the E3 returns two times the sum, and run it again.' --- import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components' import { Flow, LinkCard, LinkCards } from '@/components/ui' # Hello World Righto, here's the go. In this tutorial you're gonna get into the default template, fiddle with its FHE computation, and run the E3 again. It's for developers who've already knocked over the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), so if that's not you, off you pop and do that first. By the time you're done, your E3 spits out 2 × (a + b) instead of boring old a + b. Double the fun. And you'll know exactly which files hold the computation, its test, and its labels in the client, which is half the battle. ## Before you begin You'll want the `my-first-e3` project from the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), fresh as it came, no tinkering. Every one of the paths on this page is relative to the project folder, so park yourself in there. ## How the template computes Here's the thing: the whole FHE computation is the one Rust function, `fhe_processor`, sitting in `program/src/lib.rs`. That's it. Everything else in the template's basically a delivery driver, ferrying ciphertexts to this function and carting its result off to the committee. 1. The client locks up each number with the committee public key, encrypts it, and calls `MyProgram.publishInput`. 2. Soon as the input window shuts, the coordination server (`server/index.ts`) reads the published inputs and fires the lot off to the program server on port 13151. 3. The program server (`.interfold/support/dev/src/main.rs`) calls `fhe_processor` and sends the encrypted result straight back to the coordination server. 4. The coordination server publishes the encrypted result, and the committee decrypts it. Only the result, mind. So here's the default computation in `program/src/lib.rs`, in all its glory. We've ditched the doc comment above `policy` here to keep it short: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" use e3_compute_provider::{FHEProcessorInput, InputPolicy}; use fhe::bfv::Ciphertext; use fhe_traits::{DeserializeParametrized, Serialize}; pub fn policy() -> InputPolicy { InputPolicy::default() } /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } sum.to_bytes() } ``` - `FHEProcessorInput` has got two fields. `ciphertexts` yields `(Vec, u64)` pairs one at a time: the serialised ciphertext and its input index. `params` holds the BFV parameters of the E3. - `Ciphertext::zero` makes the zero ciphertext, the starting point. Then the `+=` operator piles each input ciphertext on top. And here's the clever bit: this addition is homomorphic. The function adds up the hidden values without ever getting a squiz at them. Like totting up a stack of sealed envelopes without opening a single one. - `sum.to_bytes()` serialises the encrypted result. - `policy()` returns the input policy. The default policy just takes every published input, no questions asked. Fair warning: the template asks for E3s with the `insecure-512` parameter set. Its plaintext modulus is 100, so every result gets worked out modulo 100. For this tutorial, keep 2 × (a + b) under 100, or you'll get some very odd answers. ## Change the computation ### Stop the stack If you've got `pnpm dev:all` humming away, give `Ctrl+C` a whack in its terminal. ### Double the encrypted sum Into `program/src/lib.rs` you go, and swap the `fhe_processor` function out for this version: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" {9-11} /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } // Add the encrypted sum to itself. The hidden value becomes 2 × (a + b). let doubled = &sum + ∑ doubled.to_bytes() } ``` `&sum + &sum` adds the two ciphertexts and hands you back a brand new ciphertext. And you don't need a single new import for it. Easy as. ### Update the unit test Down the bottom of `program/src/lib.rs` there's a test that encrypts 3 and 2 and calls `fhe_processor`. It's still expecting 5, poor thing, so bump the expected value from 5 to 10: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" let tally = Vec::::try_decode(&decrypted, Encoding::poly())?; assert_eq!(tally[0], 10); Ok(()) ``` ### Run the unit test ```bash cargo test -p e3-user-program ``` All going well, Cargo prints `test tests::test ... ok`. If the test fails, don't spit the dummy, just go back and check your `fhe_processor` against the code in the step before. ### Update the label on the input step Now the client's still telling everyone it's doing plain addition, so in `client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx`, track down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: {input1} + {input2} = ? ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: 2 × ({input1} + {input2}) = ? ``` ### Update the label on the results step Same deal over in `client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx`. Track down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2} = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `2 × (${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2}) = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` ### Start the stack ```bash pnpm dev:all ``` The `PROGRAM` process runs `interfold program start`. In dev mode that command runs `cargo run --bin e3-support-scripts-dev`, so Cargo rebuilds the program server from scratch with your shiny new `fhe_processor` baked in. ### Run an E3 Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). If the client's still hanging on to the result of an earlier E3, select **Start over** up in the top bar. Request an E3, then punch in 5 and 3. The input step shows `Ready to compute: 2 × (5 + 3) = ?`. And the results step? `2 × (5 + 3) = 16`. Sixteen, all worked out on numbers nobody could see. Not bad for a few lines of Rust. ## Why nothing else changes - **The contract.** `MyProgram.publishInput` stores a commitment for each input, and `MyProgram.verify` checks the compute proof. Neither of them has the computation anywhere in it. - **The coordination server.** `server/index.ts` passes every published input on to the program server and publishes whatever output comes back. Hasn't got a clue what the computation does, and doesn't need one. - **The deployment.** Every time it fires up, `pnpm dev:all` deploys the contracts again on a fresh local chain. In dev mode, the program server runs `fhe_processor` without a proof, and the template deploys `MockOpenVmReceiptVerifier`, which waves every receipt through on the local chain, like a bouncer who's knocked off for the night. Once you're on real proofs, though, it's a different story: `MyProgram.verify` checks the OpenVM receipt against the `imageId` that `MyProgram` gets when it's deployed. Change the program and you change that identity, so compile and deploy again. Have a geek at [Compute provider](/build/e3-program/compute-provider). ## Update the integration test There's an end-to-end test in the template too, in `tests/integration.spec.ts`. It encrypts 1 and 2 and expects their sum, and it'll be in for a shock now. So after your change, update the expected value: ```ts filename="tests/integration.spec.ts" expect(BigInt(result)).toBe(2n * (num1 + num2)) ``` Run the test with `pnpm test:integration`. Now here's the catch: this test needs a CLI that's built with the `test-only-skip-proof-aggregation` Cargo feature, and the release binaries don't come with it. So check out [Installation](/build/installation#install-the-cli) for a source build. ## Operations on ciphertexts The template uses the `fhe` crate from `gnosisguild/fhe.rs` at tag `v0.4.2`. For a `Ciphertext`, here's what that crate implements, the whole toolbox: | Operation | Operator | Example | | --------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Add two ciphertexts | `+`, `+=` | `&a + &b` | | Subtract two ciphertexts | `-`, `-=` | `&a - &b` | | Negate a ciphertext | unary `-` | `-&a` | | Add or subtract a plaintext | `+`, `+=`, `-`, `-=` | `&a + &plaintext` | | Multiply by a plaintext | `*`, `*=` | `&a * &plaintext` | One thing to watch: a `Plaintext` has to use the very same parameters object as the ciphertext, that's `fhe_inputs.params`. If the parameters objects don't match, the operator panics, and fair enough too. And every result wraps modulo the plaintext modulus. So a negative result, say from `&a - &b` with `a < b`, doesn't go below zero, it wraps right round to a big value. The crate implements `*` for two ciphertexts as well, but the default template doesn't touch it, and that's a yarn for another page. ## Next steps Write the FHE computation for your own E3 program. Validate inputs and verify proofs in your E3 program contract. Find the file to edit for each part of the template.
